newsitem.title: USA: New technique for cutting credit card debt.
newsitem.headline: New technique for cutting credit card debt.

text.p: If you're ready to start back-to-school or Christmas shopping but your credit cards still reflect last year's charges, it's time to burn the balance.
A new technique from newsletter publisher Marc Eisenson can help you pay down your credit card balances in less than half the time and less than half the interest your bank envisions.

Eisenson, publisher of "The Pocket Change Investor," in Elizaville, N.Y., suggests you put your credit card on a biweekly schedule, just as some people have put their home mortgages on a quick prepayment plan. Instead of sending the minimum due once a month when you get your credit card bill, send half the minimum due every two weeks.
Pay it off even quicker by freezing the amount you pay, even as the minimum payments required by the issuer drop with the balance.

For example. If you owe $3,500 on a credit card carrying a 17 percent interest rate and pay only the 2 percent monthly minimum (which starts at $70, but declines along with the balance), it will take you 30 years and $10,742 before you finally saw a zero balance. If, instead, you just decided to pay $35 every two weeks, you'd spend a total of $5,708 and seven years to get debt free.

Of course, you can speed it up faster than that. The theory behind Eisenson's approach is that there's no law (or even bank requirement) that says you can't make a credit card payment more often than your issuer requires you to, even if you don't have a bill.

You can send in checks at any time, as long as your credit card number is submitted with the check. Some issuers will go into your checking account and take out money on a biweekly schedule if you ask them too. You're more likely to automate the process if you pay your bills via an electronic bill paying service through your bank.

Besides offering more frequent and larger payments, you can whittle your credit card debt by transferring balances to the lowest rate card you can get or, if you are sure you'll be disciplined about paying them off, transfer the balances to a home equity line of credit that will offer a tax-deduction for your interest payments.
Send as much money as you possibly can every month, or on Eisenson's biweekly schedule, and leave your cards at home, when you start browsing through the fall-stocked aisles.
How much of a difference will these changes make?

One of the best ways to find out is to surf over to the web site offered by Kiplinger's Personal Finance magazine at www.Kiplingers.com. This site offers dozens of financial calculators, including several that will show how much money you'll save through every credit card adjustment you make. Every percentage point you drop in interest rate, every extra dollar you pay, every day you speed up an extra payment will bring you that much closer to zero.
The software at this site can help you work out a payout plan that will get you debt free on the schedule you want, or the payment level you can afford.
